# https://www.valorahq.com/financial-advisor-for-tech-employees/
Financial planning for tech employees: RSU taxes, concentrated stock, ESPP, mega backdoor Roth, IPO planning, and layoff-proofing your finances.

Financial Advisor for Tech Employees with RSUs | Valora 

 V ">

 Skip to content 

 Valora 

 For advisors 

 Find an advisor 

 Profession 
 Financial advisor for tech employees: making equity compensation actually work 
 tech employees 
 RSUs 
 stock options 
 ESPP 
 equity compensation 
 concentrated stock 
 tax planning 

 Equity compensation rewards the people who plan the route before the terrain gets steep. 

 Tech employees need planning built around equity compensation, because for many of them the equity becomes the center of the financial plan. RSUs, ESPPs, and stock options create tax problems and concentration risks that generic advice handles badly. Measured US search demand exists for this help: "financial advisor for stock options" draws 880 average monthly searches (Valora keyword ledger, Google Ads Keyword Planner 12-month averages, reviewed September 2026). This page covers what makes tech compensation different, what a specialist advisor handles, and how to choose one. 

 Key takeaways 
 Equity compensation - RSUs, ESPPs, options - is usually the largest and least understood part of a tech employee&#x27;s finances. 
 Concentration is the default risk: when your income and your wealth ride the same stock, one bad quarter hits twice. 
 Vest dates are tax events. Planning sales around vesting beats improvising them every quarter. 
 The best time to build the diversification plan is before the big vest, the IPO, or the tender offer - not after. 

 On this page 
 Why tech compensation is different 
 What a tech-focused advisor actually handles 
 The equity alphabet, in plain English 
 The concentration problem 
 Liquidity events: IPOs, tender offers, and acquisitions 
 The layoff playbook 
 The tax moves that matter most 
 What to look for when choosing 
 Questions to ask before you hire 
 The bottom line 

 Why tech compensation is different 
 A tech employee's paystub understates their financial complexity. RSUs vest as taxable income at withholding rates that often leave a surprise bill in April. The same company that pays your salary also fills your portfolio, so a bad quarter hits your income and your net worth at once. ESPP discounts, mega backdoor Roth room, 401(k) after-tax options, and deferred comp all interact. Add liquidity events - IPOs, tender offers, acquisitions - and layoffs that arrive with severance decisions and option exercise deadlines set by your plan documents, and you get a planning surface that changes every quarter. 
 The psychological side is just as unusual. Compensation arrives in grants with four-year clocks, which quietly locks people into jobs they would otherwise leave - the 'golden handcuffs' are a financial-planning fact, not a metaphor. Refresh grants, performance multipliers, and level changes keep reshaping the picture, so a plan written at hire is stale by the first vesting anniversary. And because colleagues all hold the same stock, the social pressure runs toward holding: nobody at the standup sold at vest, which makes the mechanical, unemotional choice feel strange even when it is right. 
 What a tech-focused advisor actually handles 
 Expect concrete work on: RSU sell-or-hold decisions at vest (framed as "would you buy this stock with cash today?"); diversification plans for concentrated positions, including 10b5-1 trading plans where needed; withholding gap fixes so April stops being a surprise; ESPP decisions (participating is often worth it when the discount is meaningful and cash flow allows; whether to sell promptly depends on your concentration and tax picture); mega backdoor Roth execution inside your 401(k); ISO/NSO exercise strategy and AMT exposure for startup equity; and layoff planning - severance taxation, COBRA, rollover decisions, and the option exercise deadline that catches people in their worst month. 
 Timing is the thread through all of it. Equity decisions have fixed clocks - vesting dates, ESPP purchase periods, exercise windows, blackout periods, lockup expiries - and almost every mistake in this space is a missed or misunderstood deadline rather than a bad opinion about the stock. A good advisor runs your equity as a calendar first and a portfolio second. 

 Equity comp getting complicated? 
 A conversation with the right advisor can help you see which decisions - vesting, selling, concentration - matter most right now. 
 Talk to an advisor 
 The equity alphabet, in plain English 
 RSUs are the simplest: shares that vest on a schedule and count as ordinary income when they vest, taxed like a cash bonus. The trap is withholding - companies typically withhold at the flat supplemental rate, which often under-covers high earners, which is why April brings a surprise bill. ISOs (incentive stock options) offer potential capital-gains treatment if you follow the holding rules, but exercising them can trigger the alternative minimum tax, and leaving the company starts a clock set by your grant documents - check the deadline in your plan documents immediately, because some awards allow only a short post-termination window. NSOs are simpler and less favorable: the spread at exercise is ordinary income, period. ESPPs let you buy company stock at a discount through payroll; the discount is real money, but holding the shares adds to the same concentration problem RSUs create. Each vehicle has a different tax clock, a different risk profile, and a different set of deadlines, and most employees hold two or three at once. The planning mistake is treating all of it as one blob called "my equity." 
 The concentration problem 
 When your salary, your bonus, your equity, and your career network all come from one company, you are not diversified - you are leveraged. A bad year for the company can mean a smaller bonus, a falling stock, and a layoff risk in the same quarter, and the shares you were holding for upside become the reason everything drops together. The fix is mechanical, not clever: decide what percentage of your net worth you are willing to hold in your employer's stock, set a schedule for selling down to it (many people sell RSUs at vest and never argue with themselves again), and use a 10b5-1 plan if trading windows or material information make selling awkward. None of this requires a view on the stock. It requires admitting that you already won when the shares vested, and that keeping them is a new decision, not a default. 
 Liquidity events: IPOs, tender offers, and acquisitions 
 Liquidity events reward people who planned before the headline. An IPO does not mean you can sell: lockups typically run months, blackout windows continue after, and the price at lockup expiry is anyone's guess - so the tax planning (which lots to sell, whether to exercise options early, how much to set aside for the bill) has to happen while the outcome is still uncertain. Tender offers at private companies are simpler but shorter-fused: decide your participation before the window opens, because they close fast. Acquisitions mix cash and acquirer stock and can reset vesting, so read the deal terms for your grants, not just the headline price. In all three cases the pattern is the same: the employees who do well made their rules in a calm quarter, not during the event. 

 Calculator 
 Try it: RSU withholding shortfall calculator 
 Illustrative estimates only - your real numbers depend on your full picture. 

 Related calculators: ISO exercise cost &amp; spread calculator Concentrated stock diversification timeline 401(k) contribution limit calculator 
 Book a call with an advisor 
 The layoff playbook 
 Layoffs in tech are common enough to plan for rather than fear. The financial side has a checklist: know your severance and how it is taxed, decide on COBRA versus marketplace coverage, roll over the 401(k) deliberately instead of by default, and - the one that hurts people - know your option exercise deadline, because unexercised options expire on whatever timeline your grant documents set after termination - so the first step in any layoff is reading your plan documents, in exactly the month you least want a big cash decision. The deeper defense is structural: an emergency fund measured in months of real expenses, fixed costs that a single income interruption cannot break, and a career network maintained before you need it. A good advisor builds the layoff plan while things are calm, so the event itself is an execution, not an improvisation. 
 The tax moves that matter most 
 Three tax levers do most of the work for tech employees. First, fixing the withholding gap: RSUs withheld at the flat supplemental rate routinely under-cover anyone in a high bracket, so either adjusting W-2 withholding or making estimated payments turns the April surprise into a non-event. Second, the mega backdoor Roth where the 401(k) plan allows after-tax contributions and in-plan conversion (the IRS covers the mechanics in its guidance on rollovers of after-tax contributions ) - it is the largest remaining shelter for many high earners, and it is pure process: no market call, just mechanics done correctly. Third, deliberate lot management on everything taxable: which share lots to sell, when losses offset gains, and and how charitable giving of appreciated stock can be more tax-efficient than giving cash in the right circumstances. None of this is exotic. It is the compounding value of doing ordinary tax hygiene every single year, which is exactly what equity comp makes hard to stay on top of. 
 What to look for when choosing 
 Three filters. First, fluency in equity comp mechanics: ask them to walk through RSU withholding shortfalls, the ESPP qualifying disposition rules, or ISO AMT - vague answers mean keep looking. Second, fiduciary and fee-only, so no one is earning commissions on products pitched to your concentrated position. Third, a fee model that fits: many tech employees have high income but modest current assets, so flat-fee or subscription planning often beats AUM pricing. An advisor who only wants to manage the money you have not vested yet is optimizing for themselves. 
 Red flags: an advisor who wants discretion over your whole portfolio before discussing your vesting calendar; anyone who frames holding all your employer stock as loyalty; or a pitch built around products rather than your equity calendar. And be careful with 'we specialize in your company' marketing that amounts to a seminar and a sales list - real fluency shows up in the second conversation, when they ask about your grant dates, your plan documents, and your tax return rather than your risk tolerance quiz. 
 Questions to ask before you hire 
 How many clients do you have at my company or similar ones? How do you approach RSU sell-or-hold at vest? Can you coordinate with my CPA around vesting and exercise events? How do you charge, and what do I get in year one? Have you handled a layoff or IPO for a client before? Specific, experience-based answers are the signal. 

 Make the equity actually work 
 Tell us about your grants and your goals, and we will match you with an advisor who speaks RSU fluently. 
 Find your advisor 
 The bottom line Equity compensation is a wealth engine with a tax problem and a concentration problem attached. The employees who come out ahead are not smarter about stock picks - they are earlier with the boring decisions: selling on a plan, diversifying on a schedule, and treating every vest as the taxable event it is. Whether you manage that yourself or hire help, make the rules before the next grant vests, not during it. 

 Related guides 

 Financial advisor for physicians &rarr; 
 Financial advisor for business owners &rarr; 

 Common questions 
 Should I sell my RSUs when they vest? The cleanest frame: at vest, RSUs are taxed as income, so holding them is identical to taking a cash bonus and buying your employer&#x27;s stock that day. Many planners therefore frame selling at vest and diversifying as the default, because your salary and career already depend on the company. Exceptions exist (deep conviction, upcoming catalysts), but they should be deliberate decisions sized to your total picture, not the autopilot. 
 What is the mega backdoor Roth and can I use it? It is a strategy that moves after-tax 401(k) contributions into Roth status, beyond the normal contribution limits, when your plan allows after-tax contributions and in-service conversions or distributions (IRS reference: rollovers of after-tax contributions in retirement plans (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/rollovers-of-after-tax-contributions-in-retirement-plans)). Some large tech plans allow it; many plans do not. Check your plan document or ask HR - when available, it is one of the most valuable benefits tech employees leave unused. 
 Do I need an advisor just for equity compensation? If equity is a small slice of your pay, probably not. Once RSUs or options drive most of your wealth - or you face an IPO, tender offer, or layoff with unexercised options - the tax mistakes get expensive enough that specialist advice is often worth the cost. The trigger is complexity, not account size. 
 What should I do first if I get laid off from a tech job? Handle the clock-sensitive items first: stock option exercise deadlines after departure (set by your plan and award documents - check them immediately after any departure), ESPP disposition choices, and severance timing across tax years. Then the health insurance decision (COBRA versus marketplace), then the 401(k) rollover. Most expensive mistakes happen in the first weeks, not in the long-term plan.

# https://www.valorahq.com/financial-advisor-in-houston-tx/
How to find and vet a financial advisor in Houston: Texas taxes, the energy economy, what advice costs, and how to verify credentials before you hire.

Financial advisor in Houston, TX | Valora 

 V ">

 Skip to content 

 Valora 

 For advisors 

 Find an advisor 

 City 
 Financial advisor in Houston, TX: what to know before you hire one 
 Houston 
 Texas 
 financial advisor 
 local advisor 
 energy sector 
 no state income tax 

 Finding the right advisor in Houston starts with knowing what makes money decisions here different. 

 Houston flips the usual financial-planning script: no state income tax, housing most households can still reach, and salaries that stretch - paired with an economy that can turn on a commodity price. The city counts 2,397,315 residents (Census Bureau, July 2025 estimate), and the Houston metro area's overall prices run about 1.4% below the national average (BEA regional price parities, 2024 - a metro-area measure, not city-only). Choosing a financial advisor here means finding someone who understands the energy cycle, concentrated stock risk, and what a no-income-tax state does to the standard playbook. This page covers all of it, including how to verify anyone before you hire them. 

 Key takeaways 
 Houston&#x27;s economy runs on energy, medicine, the port, and aerospace - concentrated industries mean employer stock and cycle risk belong at the center of the plan. 
 Texas levies no individual income tax, which flips standard advice: Roth moves get more attractive and property taxes carry more weight. 
 Metro-area living costs run about 1.4% below the national average (BEA 2024, a metro-level measure) and the median home value is $277,800, so Houston households can often save at rates coastal cities cannot - the plan should deploy that surplus deliberately. 
 Verifying an advisor&#x27;s record is free and takes minutes through the SEC&#x27;s public database and the Texas State Securities Board. 

 On this page 
 The Houston economy and your household balance sheet 
 No income tax: what changes and what doesn&#x27;t 
 The property tax line: homesteads and appraisals 
 When your net worth rides the energy cycle 
 What a Houston advisor actually handles 
 How Houston advisors charge, and how to compare 
 Vetting a Houston advisor: two free checks 
 Questions to ask a Houston advisor in your first meeting 

 The Houston economy and your household balance sheet 
 Houston's economy is unusually concentrated in big, cyclical industries. Energy still sets the tone - oil and gas majors, oilfield services, pipeline and trading firms - and with it comes compensation built on bonuses, stock awards, and cycles that can turn fast. Around energy sits the Texas Medical Center, one of the world's largest medical complexes, a port economy that moves a meaningful share of US trade, and NASA's Johnson Space Center with its contractor ecosystem. Many Houston households earn well while depending heavily on one industry's fortunes, and often on one employer's stock. 
 The household numbers frame the opportunity. The median household income is $64,813 and the median owner-occupied home value is $277,800 (Census Bureau, 2020-2024) - a ratio between income and housing costs that coastal cities lost years ago. With metro prices just under the national average, a disciplined Houston household can save at rates that are genuinely hard to reach in New York or San Francisco. The typical planning conversation here is less about stretching to cover fixed costs and more about deploying the surplus well: how much company stock is too much, how to handle a bonus-heavy income, and how to build wealth that survives the energy cycle. 
 One more Houston reality belongs on the balance sheet: weather. The region's flood exposure is documented in detail - FEMA publishes flood studies for Harris County and maintains a public flood-map portal - which makes flood insurance, a real emergency fund, and knowing what your homeowner's policy does not cover part of basic financial hygiene here. Advisors who work with Houston families treat disaster resilience as a planning line item, not an afterthought. 
 No income tax: what changes and what doesn't 
 Texas does not levy an individual income tax , and Houston adds no local income tax on top. That single fact reshapes several standard planning moves. Roth conversions and Roth contributions are often more attractive when your marginal rate is federal-only. There is no state-level tax break to chase with retirement contributions, so the federal math drives the decision. And if you moved to Texas from a high-tax state, the raise in take-home pay is real - but states fund themselves one way or another, and Texas leans heavily on property and sales taxes. Texas also has no state estate tax, which leaves the federal rules as the relevant frame for most families. 
 One nuance worth knowing: many Houstonians are not lifetime Texans. If you spent part of your career in a state with an income tax - or might return to one - the timing of bonuses, equity events, and retirement moves around a relocation can change your lifetime tax bill meaningfully. That timing is fact-specific and worth mapping with a professional before the move, not after. 
 The property tax line: homesteads and appraisals 
 What Texas skips in income tax it collects elsewhere, and homeowners meet that trade directly in the mail each year. Property taxes are set locally - county, school district, city, and special districts layering together - so two similar houses a few miles apart can carry noticeably different bills. The state does offer relief on a primary residence, but none of it is automatic. Homestead exemptions reduce the taxable value of your home and generally must be applied for , and state law limits how quickly a homestead's appraised value can rise, with conditions . Appraisals can also be protested, which is why many Houston homeowners treat the annual appraisal notice as a financial to-do rather than junk mail. When you compare suburbs, the all-in tax rate belongs in the comparison next to the house price; a good advisor or realtor will run that number with you. 
 When your net worth rides the energy cycle 
 Houston's signature financial risk is concentration: the same industry that pays the salary often fills the brokerage account. An engineer at an oilfield services firm might hold restricted stock in her employer, a pension tied to the same sector, and a bonus linked to the same commodity price - triple exposure to one cycle. When energy turns down, the job, the stock, and the bonus can sag together, which is exactly when selling shares hurts most. 
 The counterweight is deliberate diversification, and it is harder than it sounds. Employer stock can bring trading-window limits and tax consequences. A written plan can help you compare whether, when, and how to reduce a concentrated position; the answer depends on your grants, basis, restrictions, and goals. Some Houston families add a fourth leg of exposure without noticing - mineral rights or royalty interests inherited or bought over the years - which may also be worth including in an exposure inventory and discussing with an advisor. This is the conversation a Houston advisor should lead with; if yours never raises it, that tells you something. 

 Calculator 
 Try it: State-aware paycheck calculator (Texas) 
 Illustrative estimates only - your real numbers depend on your full picture. 

 Related calculators: Retirement savings growth calculator Withdrawal amount calculator 
 Book a call with an advisor 
 What a Houston advisor actually handles 
 Beyond generic portfolio management, the working list for a Houston advisor usually includes: 

 Concentrated stock and employer risk. Systematic diversification plans that respect trading windows, taxes, and vesting schedules - built before the cycle turns, not after. 
 Bonus and cycle planning. Smoothing a commodity-linked income into steady saving, debt payoff, and investing, with reserves sized for downturns that can last more than a quarter. 
 Retirement strategy in a no-income-tax state. Roth versus traditional decisions, conversion timing, and withdrawal sequencing when only the federal rules apply. 
 Property tax and housing strategy. Homestead exemption and appraisal-protest awareness, plus all-in rate comparisons across suburbs and districts. 
 Disaster resilience. Flood insurance gaps, emergency reserves, and document readiness as standing agenda items. 
 Physician and medical professional planning. The Medical Center employs a small city's worth of high earners with late-start careers, student debt, and practice-ownership decisions. 
 Business, mineral, and royalty interests. Coordinating family partnerships, royalty income, and operating businesses with estate and tax professionals. 

 If an advisor's plan for you reads like it was written for a high-tax coastal city, they have not understood the assignment. 

 Not sure where your plan stands? 
 One conversation can show you how exposed your plan is to a single stock or a single cycle - and what to do about it first. 
 Talk to an advisor 
 How Houston advisors charge, and how to compare 
 Fee conversations in Houston often start with a project rather than a portfolio. Untangling a concentrated stock position or setting up a diversification plan is defined work, and many advisors will quote it as a flat project fee or an hourly engagement before any ongoing arrangement. Ongoing advice usually follows the standard models: a percentage of assets managed (commonly around 1% a year nationally, often lower as balances grow) or a flat annual fee. No reliable data tracks a Houston-specific average, so the useful comparisons are structural: ask each candidate what the first twelve months of work look like and what they cost, get the full fee schedule in writing, and ask whether they earn commissions on products they recommend alongside their fee. An advisor who can itemize the work is easier to compare than one who quotes a single percentage. 
 Vetting a Houston advisor: two free checks 
 Before any interview, run two searches. The first is the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure database: the advisor's name or firm pulls up registration status, employment history, disclosed disciplinary events, and the Form ADV brochure describing services, fees, and conflicts in the firm's own words. The second is the Texas State Securities Board , which regulates advisors operating in the state, publishes enforcement actions, and takes investor complaints - its public records can surface state-level issues that never reached the federal level. Neither check costs anything or takes more than a few minutes. Then, in the room: Are you a fiduciary at all times? Fee-only or fee-based? Who will I actually work with? 

 Ready to find your advisor in Houston? 
 Tell us what you are working toward and we will match you with an advisor who understands how Houston wealth is actually built. 
 Find your advisor 
 Questions to ask a Houston advisor in your first meeting 

 A lot of my net worth is tied to my employer and the energy cycle. How would you build a diversification plan for me, and what would it cost? 
 How does your tax planning change for clients in a no-income-tax state - Roth decisions, conversions, withdrawal sequencing? 
 Do you factor flood risk and insurance gaps into your planning? 
 How many of your clients work in energy, medicine, or engineering, and what did you set up for them? 
 Are you a fiduciary at all times, and are you fee-only? How exactly are you paid, and what would the first year of work together cost? 
 At what point would you bring in a CPA or estate attorney - say for business-sale planning or Texas estate documents - and how do you coordinate with them? 

 The right Houston advisor treats concentration risk, the energy cycle, and the no-income-tax playbook as the core of the plan - not as footnotes to a national template.

 Common questions 
 How much does a financial advisor in Houston cost? It depends on the work. Defined projects like a stock-diversification plan are often quoted flat or hourly; ongoing management is usually a percentage of assets (commonly around 1% a year nationally) or a flat annual fee. No reliable data tracks a Houston-specific average, so ask each candidate to itemize the first year of work and its cost, in writing, and compare those side by side. 
 Do I need a local advisor in Houston, or can I work with one remotely? Location matters less than fit and credentials. An advisor who understands Texas taxes and the energy and medical economies can serve you well remotely; a local office is a preference, not a requirement. Verify any advisor - local or remote - through the SEC&#x27;s public database before hiring. 
 How do I check if a Houston financial advisor is legitimate? Run two free searches: the SEC&#x27;s Investment Adviser Public Disclosure site (adviserinfo.sec.gov) for registration, disciplinary history, and Form ADV, and the Texas State Securities Board for state-level enforcement and complaints. Both take minutes. 
 What should a financial plan in Houston account for? At minimum: Texas&#x27;s lack of an individual income tax (which reshapes Roth and conversion decisions), property taxes and homestead mechanics, employer stock concentration in the energy and medical sectors, flood risk and insurance gaps, and housing costs in a market where the median home value is $277,800. A plan built on national averages misses what actually shapes your finances here.

# https://www.valorahq.com/financial-advisor-in-new-york-ny/
How to find and vet a financial advisor in New York: NY state and city taxes, local cost of living, what advice costs, and how to verify credentials before you hire.

Financial advisor in New York, NY | Valora 

 V ">

 Skip to content 

 Valora 

 For advisors 

 Find an advisor 

 City 
 Financial advisor in New York, NY: what to know before you hire one 
 New York 
 New York City 
 NYC 
 financial advisor 
 local advisor 
 New York taxes 

 Finding the right advisor in New York starts with knowing what makes money decisions here different. 

 New York packs more financial contradictions into one zip code than most cities see in a lifetime: top-tier incomes against top-tier costs, a state tax and a city tax stacked together, and careers where a single bonus can outweigh a whole year's salary. The city counts 8,584,629 residents (Census Bureau, July 2025 estimate) and living costs about 12.6% above the national average (BEA regional price parities for the New York metro area, 2024 - a metro-level measure, not city-only). If you are looking for a financial advisor here, the useful questions are local ones: how they handle the tax stack, what they know about bonus- and equity-driven pay, and whether their advice accounts for what housing actually costs in the five boroughs. This page walks through all of it, including how to verify anyone before you hire them. 

 Key takeaways 
 New York&#x27;s economy runs on finance, healthcare, tech, and professional services - compensation here often means bonuses, equity, and K-1s, and the right advisor plans around that. 
 New York State revised its income tax brackets for 2026, and NYC residents pay a separate city income tax on top - one of the heaviest combined tax stacks in the country, which changes Roth, conversion, and residency math. 
 New York State&#x27;s estate tax exclusion is $7,350,000 in 2026, below the federal level, so ordinary city wealth can trip state estate tax. 
 Verifying an advisor&#x27;s record is free and takes minutes through the SEC&#x27;s public database and the NY Attorney General&#x27;s Investor Protection Bureau. 

 On this page 
 What makes financial planning in New York different 
 The New York tax stack: state, city, and estate 
 The co-op question, and other New York housing math 
 What a New York advisor actually handles 
 What advice costs in a city like this 
 Checking a New York advisor&#x27;s record 
 Questions to ask a New York advisor in your first meeting 

 What makes financial planning in New York different 
 New York's economy concentrates unusually high-earning, unusually complex compensation. Wall Street still sets the tone: bonus-heavy pay, deferred comp, carried interest, and restricted stock are ordinary here in a way they are not in most cities. Around finance sits a deep bench of hospitals and health systems, a large technology sector, law and consulting firms, media, and universities - industries where equity awards, partnership structures, and uneven annual income are common. A plan built for a steady biweekly paycheck under-serves a household whose income arrives in a March bonus or a K-1 distribution. 
 The household numbers frame the challenge. The median household income is $80,483 and the median owner-occupied home value is $777,600 (Census Bureau, 2020-2024). Only about a third of households own their homes. That combination - solid incomes against some of the country's highest housing costs - means the typical New York planning conversation is about competing claims on cash flow: rent or buy at city prices, how much house is too much, whether to stay in the city or plan around an eventual move, and how to keep retirement saving on track while carrying big-city fixed costs. Because regional prices run roughly 12.6% above the national average, a savings rate that looks healthy elsewhere can quietly underperform here. 
 The New York tax stack: state, city, and estate 
 New York State's income tax is progressive, and the brackets were revised for 2026 under legislation enacted in 2025 . Most filers fall in the single-digit brackets; the state's highest-rate method kicks in only above about $1.08 million of income . On top of that, New York City residents pay a separate city personal income tax , collected by the state, with its own current rate tables . Two planning consequences follow. First, the combined state-plus-city marginal rate changes real decisions: Roth versus traditional contributions, the timing of Roth conversions, and how valuable each pre-tax dollar of 401(k) space is. Second, residency itself becomes a financial decision. Moving a few miles changes your tax picture, and New York examines residency claims closely - if a move is part of your plan, the details of when and how you establish the new domicile matter, and that is specialist-CPA territory. 
 Two more New York specifics belong in most plans. Retirement income gets meaningful relief under current New York rules: pensions from New York State and local governments and the federal government are generally not taxed by New York State , and residents who are 59 and a half or older for the entire tax year may exclude up to $20,000 of qualified pension and annuity income (New York State DTF retiree guidance, checked September 2026). And New York has its own estate tax, with a basic exclusion of $7,350,000 for deaths in 2026 - below the federal level, so families with a city apartment, retirement accounts, and life insurance can cross into state estate tax exposure without feeling wealthy. Whether that applies to you depends on the size and structure of your estate, and it is worth mapping early. 
 The co-op question, and other New York housing math 
 Housing dominates New York finances in a way outsiders rarely appreciate. Much of the city's owned housing stock is co-operative rather than condominium, and buying into a co-op means passing a board's financial review, not just a lender's. A board may review a buyer's finances in detail - down payment, post-closing liquidity, debt-to-income limits - and the requirements vary building by building, so the only way to know a given co-op's bar is to ask before you offer. Condos trade those hurdles for higher prices and their own fee structures. Then there is the renter's version of the problem: with most households renting, plenty of high earners build wealth entirely outside housing, which makes their investment plan carry the load a mortgage would elsewhere. 
 The planning consequences are concrete. A home purchase here interacts with everything else: the down payment competes with retirement contributions, the carrying costs set the floor for your emergency fund. Mortgage interest and property taxes can affect the rent-versus-buy comparison; check which costs apply to your situation. An advisor working with New York clients should be fluent in all of it - including telling you when the honest answer is that buying does not pencil out yet.

 Illustrative estimates only - your real numbers depend on your full picture.

 Book a call with an advisor 
 What a New York advisor actually handles 
 Beyond generic portfolio management, the working list for a New York advisor usually includes: 

 Compensation design around the bonus cycle. Smoothing a March-bonus income into year-round saving, taxes, and investment contributions - and deciding what to do with deferred comp and equity before it decides for you. 
 Tax-aware account strategy across the state-plus-city stack. Roth versus traditional decisions, conversion timing in lower-income years, and asset location that respects the combined marginal rate. 
 Housing decisions at New York prices. Co-op board financial preparation, rent-versus-buy analysis, jumbo mortgage coordination, and how a purchase fits next to retirement saving rather than instead of it. 
 Residency and relocation planning. For the many New Yorkers whose five-year plan involves leaving - timing income, equity events, and retirement moves around the change, with a CPA handling the audit-sensitive details. 
 Estate planning above the New York exclusion. Coordinating beneficiary designations, trusts, and insurance with an attorney when an estate may exceed $7.35 million. 
 Retirement income sequencing. Making full use of New York's pension exclusions when drawing down accounts. 

 If an advisor's plan for you looks identical to the one they would hand a client in a no-tax state, they have not understood the assignment. 

 Not sure where your plan stands? 
 One conversation can show you how the tax stack, housing math, and your pay cycle fit together - and what to fix first. 
 Talk to an advisor 
 What advice costs in a city like this 
 New York has every flavor of advisory pricing, which makes comparison-shopping worth the effort. The three models you will meet most often: a percentage of assets under management (commonly around 1% a year nationally, often lower as balances grow), a flat annual or project fee for defined planning work, or an hourly rate for one-off questions. One New York wrinkle worth knowing: firms here frequently set account minimums, and the minimum can matter more than the rate - a low percentage at a firm whose minimum you barely clear can cost more attention than money. Published industry surveys keep most fee arrangements within a predictable national range, but no reliable data tracks a New York-specific average, so treat any figure as a starting range, not a quote. Ask every candidate for their full fee schedule in writing, their minimums, and whether they earn commissions on products they recommend alongside their fee. 
 Checking a New York advisor's record 
 Start with the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure site. Search the advisor's name or firm and you get their registration status, employment history, any disclosed disciplinary events, and the Form ADV brochure - services, fees, and conflicts in the firm's own words. New York adds a second layer: the Attorney General's Investor Protection Bureau enforces the state's securities laws and takes investor complaints. Both checks are free and take minutes. After that, the interview questions that matter: Are you a fiduciary at all times? Are you fee-only or fee-based? Who exactly manages my account day to day? 

 Ready to find your advisor in New York? 
 Tell us what you are working toward and we will match you with an advisor who knows how New York money actually works. 
 Find your advisor 
 Questions to ask a New York advisor in your first meeting 

 How do you handle the New York State plus City tax stack in your planning - Roth decisions, conversion timing, asset location? 
 How many of your clients are paid on a bonus or equity cycle like mine, and what did you set up for them? 
 Have you helped clients through co-op board financial reviews or New York rent-versus-buy decisions? 
 If I leave New York in the next few years, how would you help me plan around the move? 
 Are you a fiduciary at all times, and are you fee-only? What are your minimums, and how exactly are you paid? 
 At what point would you bring in a CPA or estate attorney - for example, if my estate could approach New York's estate-tax exclusion - and how do you coordinate with them? 

 The right New York advisor treats the city's tax stack, housing math, and compensation cycles as the core of the plan - not as footnotes to a national template. 

 Related guides 

 Financial advisor for business owners &rarr; 
 Financial advisor for tech employees &rarr; 

 Common questions 
 How much does a financial advisor in New York cost? Expect the three standard models: a percentage of assets managed (commonly around 1% a year nationally), a flat planning fee, or an hourly rate. In New York, account minimums often matter as much as the rate, since many firms set high floors. No reliable data tracks a city-specific average, so compare written fee schedules and minimums from each candidate rather than relying on any quoted range. 
 Do I need a local advisor in New York, or can I work with one remotely? Location matters less than fit and credentials. An advisor who understands the New York State and City tax stack and your profession can serve you well remotely; a local office is a preference, not a requirement. Verify any advisor - local or remote - through the SEC&#x27;s public database before hiring. 
 How do I check if a New York financial advisor is legitimate? Search their name or firm on the SEC&#x27;s Investment Adviser Public Disclosure site (adviserinfo.sec.gov) for registration, disciplinary history, and Form ADV. For a second layer, the New York Attorney General&#x27;s Investor Protection Bureau handles state enforcement and complaints. Both are free. 
 What should a financial plan in New York account for? At minimum: the state-plus-city income tax stack, the state estate tax exclusion ($7,350,000 in 2026), housing costs in a market where the median home value is $777,600 and most households rent, and the bonus- and equity-driven compensation that powers the city&#x27;s economy. A plan built on national averages misses what actually shapes your finances here.

 Cookie and Analytics Notice 

 Effective date: September 28, 2026 

 On this page 
 What cookies are 
 What the Site uses 
 What the Site does not use 
 Your choices 
 Changes to this notice 
 Contact 

 This notice explains how Valora uses cookies and similar technologies on valorahq.com (the "Site"). It should be read together with our Privacy Policy. 
 What cookies are 
 Cookies are small text files a website stores on your device. Similar technologies, such as browser local storage, serve the same purpose: remembering a device between visits so the site works and so we can understand how it is used. 
 What the Site uses 

 Strictly necessary storage. Required for the Site to load and function securely. You cannot opt out of these without breaking the Site. 
 Analytics (PostHog). We use PostHog to understand how the Site is used: which pages are viewed, how visitors move through the Site, and what content is useful. PostHog stores a first-party identifier (a cookie and/or local storage entry whose name begins with "ph_") so it can recognize a returning device. This identifier is tied to browsing activity on this Site only; we do not use it to track you elsewhere. 
 Third-party forms (Google Forms). The readiness check is powered by Google Forms. When you open the form, Google may set its own cookies under its own privacy policy. We do not control those cookies. 

 What the Site does not use 
 We do not use advertising cookies, retargeting pixels, social-media trackers, or any third-party ad network. Nothing on this Site profiles you for advertising. 
 Your choices 

 Browser controls. Most browsers let you block or delete cookies. Blocking the analytics identifier does not affect how the Site works for you. 
 Clearing stored data. You can remove the PostHog identifier at any time by clearing cookies and site data for valorahq.com in your browser settings; you will then be counted as a new visitor on your next visit. 
 Google's cookies. Manage Google's cookies through your browser or Google's own settings. 

 Changes to this notice 
 We may update this notice as the Site's tooling changes and will revise the effective date when we do. 
 Contact 
 Questions about cookies and analytics: barot@valorahq.com .

 Changes to this Policy 
 Contact 

 This Privacy Policy explains what information Valora ("Valora," "we," "us," or "our") collects through the website at valorahq.com (the "Site"), how we use and share it, and the choices and rights you have. The Site is directed at users located in the United States and is operated under United States law. 
 Information you give us 

 Contact form. When you contact us, we collect the information you submit, typically your name, email address, and the contents of your message. 
 Readiness check. The readiness check is powered by Google Forms. The answers you choose to provide, which may include details about your financial situation and goals, are submitted to Google and then stored in an internal spreadsheet we use to respond to you and, where you ask, to suggest advisor matches. Google's own privacy policy applies to its handling of the form. 
 Email. If you email us, we keep your address and correspondence. 

 Please do not send us highly sensitive information such as Social Security numbers, account numbers, or passwords. The Site is not designed to receive them. 
 Information collected automatically 
 We use PostHog, an analytics product, on every page of the Site. PostHog collects standard usage data: pages viewed, interactions (such as clicks and form starts), referring pages, approximate geographic location derived from your IP address, and device and browser characteristics. PostHog identifies returning visitors using a first-party cookie and/or your browser's local storage. Our Cookie and Analytics Notice has the details, including how to opt out. 
 What we do not collect 
 The Site has no user accounts and no passwords, processes no payments, and carries no advertising. We do not collect payment card data, we do not run advertising or retargeting trackers, and we do not buy data about you from data brokers. 
 How we use information 

 To respond to your inquiries and operate the matching and introduction process you ask for. 
 To operate, maintain, secure, and improve the Site and its content. 
 To understand aggregate usage so we can make the Site more useful. 
 To comply with law and protect our rights and the rights of others. 

 We do not sell your personal information, and we do not share it for cross-context behavioral advertising. 
 How information is shared 

 Service providers. We share information with the vendors that run the Site: PostHog (analytics), Google (forms and internal documents), and our hosting provider. They process information on our behalf under their own terms. 
 Advisors, at your request. If you ask to be introduced or matched, we share the information you provided for that purpose with the advisor or advisors involved, so they can respond to you. 
 Legal and safety. We may disclose information where required by law, regulation, or legal process, or to protect the rights, property, or safety of Valora, our users, or others. 
 Business transfers. If Valora is involved in a merger, acquisition, or sale of assets, information may be transferred as part of that transaction, subject to this Policy. 

 Retention 
 We keep contact and readiness-check information for as long as needed to respond to you and operate the service, and analytics data for the retention period configured in our analytics tools. We delete or de-identify information when it is no longer needed for these purposes, unless the law requires us to keep it. 
 Security 
 We use reasonable administrative and technical safeguards for the information we hold, including limiting access to those who need it. No method of transmission or storage is completely secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security. 
 Your privacy rights 
 Regardless of where you live in the United States, you may ask us to: access the personal information we hold about you; correct inaccurate information; or delete your information. Email barot@valorahq.com with your request. We may need to verify your identity before acting, and we will respond within the time required by applicable law (and in any event within 45 days). 
 State privacy rights. If you live in a state with a comprehensive privacy law, such as California (CCPA/CPRA), Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, or others, you may have additional rights, including the right to know the categories and specific pieces of personal information we have collected, the right to delete and correct it, the right to opt out of its sale or sharing, and the right not to be discriminated against for exercising your rights. As stated above, we do not sell personal information or share it for cross-context behavioral advertising, so there is no sale or sharing to opt out of. To exercise any state right, email barot@valorahq.com . 
 Do Not Track. We do not currently respond to browser Do Not Track signals. You can limit analytics collection through the browser and cookie controls described in our Cookie and Analytics Notice. 
 Children's privacy 
 The Site is intended for adults and is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13. If you believe a child has provided us information, contact us and we will delete it. 
 Visitors from outside the United States 
 The Site is intended for United States users. If you visit from elsewhere, you understand that your information will be processed in the United States and in other countries where our service providers operate, whose laws may differ from yours. 
 Changes to this Policy 
 We may update this Policy from time to time and will revise the effective date when we do. Material changes take effect when posted unless stated otherwise. 
 Contact 
 Privacy questions and requests: barot@valorahq.com .

It does not take into account your objectives, financial situation, or needs, and it is not a recommendation, offer, or solicitation to buy or sell any security or to adopt any strategy. 
 Your use of the Site, including submitting a contact form or completing the readiness check, does not create an advisory, fiduciary, attorney-client, accountant-client, or any other professional relationship between you and Valora. No attorney-client relationship is created by anything on this Site or by contacting us. Any advisory relationship you form is solely between you and the advisor you engage, under the terms you agree with them. 
 Before making any financial, legal, or tax decision, consult a qualified professional who understands your specific circumstances. 
 Advisor directory and listings 
 Some advisor profiles and directory listings on the Site are compiled from publicly available sources, such as regulatory filings and the advisors' own published materials. We work to keep this information accurate and current, but we do not guarantee that any listing is complete, accurate, or up to date, and information may change without notice to us. 
 Inclusion in the directory reflects our editorial judgment about relevance to a topic or audience. It is not a guarantee of quality, performance, or outcomes, and it should not be your only basis for choosing an advisor. Always verify an advisor's registration status, disciplinary history, and credentials independently, including through the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure database and FINRA BrokerCheck. 
 If you are an advisor or firm listed on the Site and you believe your listing is inaccurate or outdated, or you want it corrected or removed, email us at barot@valorahq.com . We will review reasonable correction and removal requests promptly. 
 Matching and the readiness check 
 When you submit a contact form or complete the readiness check, the information you provide is used to respond to you and, where you ask for it, to suggest or arrange an introduction to one or more independent advisors. We do not guarantee that any match, introduction, or advisor will be right for you, that any advisor will accept you as a client, or that any particular outcome will result. 
 Any engagement, fee arrangement, or agreement you enter into with an advisor is strictly between you and that advisor. Valora is not a party to it and has no responsibility or liability arising from it. 
 Calculators and estimates 
 The calculators on the Site produce simplified estimates based on the inputs you provide and stated assumptions. They are illustrations only: they ignore many real-world variables, they are not predictions, and they must not be relied on as financial, tax, or investment advice. Actual results will differ. 
 Your submissions 
 You are responsible for the accuracy of information you submit through the Site. Please do not send us sensitive personal information such as Social Security numbers, account numbers, passwords, or full statements; the Site is not designed to receive them, and you send any such information at your own risk. 
 By submitting content to the Site (for example, a question through the contact form), you grant Valora a non-exclusive, royalty-free right to use that submission to operate the Site and respond to you. We do not publish your submissions or use them in marketing without your permission. 
 Acceptable use 
 You agree not to: (a) use the Site for any unlawful purpose; (b) scrape, crawl, or bulk-copy the Site or its content by automated means without our written permission; (c) interfere with or disrupt the Site, its security, or its infrastructure; (d) misrepresent your identity or affiliation; or (e) use the Site's content to build a competing directory or service. 
 Intellectual property 
 The Site and its original content, including text, design, graphics, and the Valora name and logo, are owned by or licensed to Valora and are protected by United States and international intellectual property laws. We grant you a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable license to access and view the Site for your personal, non-commercial use. You may not reproduce, distribute, modify, or create derivative works from Site content without our prior written consent, except as permitted by law. Names, logos, and trademarks of advisors and firms mentioned on the Site belong to their respective owners. 
 Third-party services and links 
 The Site relies on third-party services, including Google Forms (which powers the readiness check) and PostHog (our analytics provider), and may link to third-party websites. We do not control and are not responsible for the content, policies, or practices of third-party services or sites. Your use of them is governed by their own terms and privacy policies.

# https://www.valorahq.com/team/
Meet the team behind Valora's content, tools, and research - who does what, and who says no.

Team | Valora 

 V ">

 Skip to content 

 Valora 

 For advisors 

 Find an advisor 

 Company 
 Team 

 Valora is built by a small team with very clear ownership - everyone on this page can tell you exactly what they're responsible for, because we wrote it down. The work splits into content, quality, engineering, growth, and the people who keep all of it pointed in the same direction. Questions about the site or the work: barot@valorahq.com . 
 The team 
 Leadership 
 Sam Nakamura Chief Technology Officer Sam builds and runs valorahq.com: the pages, the calculators, and the machinery that keeps them fast, findable, and honest about what they can&#x27;t do. He grew up in Vancouver and taught himself to code by building sites for local bands at fourteen - the bands broke up, the habit stuck - and spent the next decade keeping infrastructure alive at startups that grew faster than their servers. His badass credential: he treats a slow page load as a personal insult and has the uptime record to prove it. Away from the keyboard he builds other keyboards, rides his bike at off-peak hours, and holds strong opinions about coffee extraction. 
 Clara Nguyen Chief Operating Officer Clara keeps the team&#x27;s operations running day to day: the schedules, the systems, and the hundred small decisions that nobody notices until they go wrong. They don&#x27;t go wrong. She grew up in San Jose in a family that ran a restaurant, which is where she learned that operations is mostly caring about details other people find boring. Before Valora she ran ops at a startup that scaled from twelve people to two hundred without losing its receipts - hers, mostly. Her badass credential: vendor renewals, onboarding checklists, and folder logic all bend to her systems. Outside work she throws pottery, plans vacations with color-coded itineraries, and finds your lack of a backup plan quietly stressful. 
 Jordan Blake Chief of Staff Jordan coordinates work across the team and keeps projects moving: priorities, handoffs, and the gentle art of asking &quot;what&#x27;s the status?&quot; until there is one. He&#x27;s from Chicago, came up through consulting, and left for startups after realizing he liked the work but not the decks about the work. His badass credential: he is the team&#x27;s institutional memory - if a decision was made in a meeting six weeks ago, Jordan can tell you what it was, why, and who owes the next step. If two parts of this site feel like they were made by the same company, Jordan is a large part of why. Off the clock he climbs, hosts board-game night where his rulings are final, and keeps a to-do list for his to-do lists. 
 Elena Voss Executive Assistant, Office of the Founder Elena runs the Office of the Founder: the calendar, the priorities, and the polite but immovable &quot;he doesn&#x27;t have that slot.&quot; She grew up in the Netherlands and learned English partly from American courtroom dramas, which explains both her vocabulary and her negotiating style. She has supported founders and executives across two continents and can spot a scheduling conflict three weeks before it happens. Her badass credential: she turns a founder&#x27;s hundred ideas into the ten that actually happen, in order, with buffers. Outside work she does pilates, reads thrillers, and maintains the only truly empty inbox known to science - hers. 
 Content 
 Lena Ortiz Head of Content Lena researches and writes everything you can read on Valora: the guides, the articles, and the niche pages that explain what a financial advisor actually does for your specific profession. She&#x27;s from Austin, started as a local-news reporter, and traded city hall for personal finance after discovering that tax brackets generate better reader mail than zoning boards. Her badass credential: she has now thought deeply about the finances of forty-nine different professions and can explain self-employment tax to a merchant mariner in that mariner&#x27;s own vocabulary. The job is equal parts research, writing, and cheerfully deleting the third draft. Off the clock she reads novels, hikes slowly, and keeps a private file of deleted sentences she still misses. 
 Mira Head of Content Quality Mira reviews every piece of content before it ships: the facts, the sources, and whether the rules it cites are still the rules. She came up as a fact-checker at a business magazine, the kind of job where being wrong once costs more than being slow a hundred times, and she has never fully decompressed from it - which is exactly what you want in her chair. Her badass credential: she is the reason a Valora page says &quot;conditions apply&quot; instead of &quot;trust us,&quot; and she has never once said &quot;looks fine&quot; on the first read. Our accuracy record is her personality, institutionalized. Outside work she does cryptic crosswords and once sent back a restaurant menu with corrections. She tipped well, though. 
 Iris Chen Head of Newsletter &amp; Media Outreach Iris runs Valora&#x27;s newsletter and media outreach: getting Valora&#x27;s work and point of view into the inboxes and conversations people are already paying attention to. She&#x27;s from Seattle, where she started in public radio - cutting tape, booking guests, learning what makes someone actually listen - before moving into media relations for startups. Her badass credential: she pitches less like a publicist and more like a listener who knows what each show needs next, which is why the bookings keep coming. She knows which shows your commute depends on and which newsletters actually get read. Off duty she&#x27;s at live shows, keeps a podcast queue longer than a cross-country drive, and makes playlists for every occasion including &quot;waiting.&quot; 
 Growth 
 Owen Price Head of Growth &amp; Partnerships Owen leads Valora&#x27;s backlink and authority work: earning the partnerships, citations, and links that put Valora in front of more of the people it can help. He&#x27;s originally from Cardiff and has the rare Welsh talent of making a business call feel like catching up with an old friend. He spent years building partner programs at SaaS companies before Valora. His badass credential: his calendar is a masterclass in time zones, his definition of a good meeting is one that ends with a next step, and he keeps a running note on everyone Valora should know. Off the calendar he plays squash, cooks for more people than the recipe intended, and loses arguments about which airport lounge is best. 
 Arjun Mehta Head of Consumer Growth Arjun leads Valora&#x27;s consumer growth and AI search work - how people find Valora, and how Valora shows up when they ask AI assistants and search engines their money questions. He grew up in Bangalore, trained as a search engineer, and watched the industry he mastered get rebuilt by AI in real time - so he rebuilt his own expertise to match. His badass credential: he thinks about how machines read so that humans get better answers, and he can tell you not just where search is going but what it will reward when it gets there. Search changed, so his job exists. After hours he plays blitz chess, reads science fiction, and explains recommendation algorithms to relatives who didn&#x27;t ask. 
 MR Marcus Reed Head of Advisor Growth Leads Valora&#x27;s advisor growth plan, from outreach and advisor content to qualified calls and paid advisor revenue. Keeps each channel measured against the same pipeline and revenue scorecard. 
 Ethan Brooks Head of Outbound Ethan runs Valora&#x27;s outbound work, connecting with advisors and partners who should know what we&#x27;re building. He&#x27;s from Dallas, started as the most junior rep on a forty-person sales floor, and outlasted, out-called, and out-organized his way to running outreach himself. His badass credential: he tracks every conversation the way other people track fantasy stats - who replied, when, and exactly what the right next touch is - so the right people hear about Valora from an actual human, on a cadence that never slips. Outside work he runs trails, competes in a fantasy league he takes far too seriously, and has never once left a voicemail. 
 Media &amp; Community 
 Evelyn Hart Head of PR Evelyn leads PR: the press relationships and the version of the Valora story that travels further than we can carry it ourselves. She&#x27;s a born New Yorker who started in newsrooms when fax machines were still load-bearing, moved to the agency side, and has now placed stories across two decades of media that stopped existing and the outlets that replaced them. Her badass credential: her contacts book spans twenty years of editors, and they still take her calls because she only ever sends stories, never pitches. Off deadline she goes to opening nights, writes actual letters with stamps, and can name the best croissant in three cities. 
 Sofia Mensah Earned Media Lead Sofia runs earned media: getting Valora covered because the work deserves it, not because we asked twice. She was born in Accra and raised in London, started in music journalism, and moved into tech communications when she realized the startups had better stories than the bands. Her badass credential: she knows the difference between a pitch and a story at a glance, editors answer her because she only sends the second kind, and every placement she wins becomes a relationship instead of a transaction. Outside work she collects vinyl, devours long-form radio documentaries, and knows the backstory of every song she plays you. 
 Miles Carter Podcast Lead Miles books the podcasts: matching Valora&#x27;s point of view with the shows whose audiences will actually care. He&#x27;s from Nashville, where he started as an audio engineer in studios that smelled of coffee and tube amps, and moved into podcast production when the industry found its second golden age. His badass credential: he listens to more episodes before breakfast than most people finish in a month - research, he calls it, and he&#x27;s not wrong - so his pitches land because he already knows the host&#x27;s last ten guests. Off mic he tinkers with his home studio, makes his own hot sauce, and rates every room by its acoustics. 
 Noah Kim Reddit Community Lead Noah runs Valora&#x27;s Reddit community: showing up in the subreddits where people ask real money questions and answering like a person, not a pitch. He&#x27;s from Los Angeles, spent years managing communities for gaming companies - the internet&#x27;s most demanding audiences - and developed an unshakeable sense of what a community will and will not tolerate. His badass credential: he knows each subreddit&#x27;s rules, culture, and moderators cold, and his answers read like the best kind of comment thread: specific, patient, and free of anything that sounds like marketing. Outside work he plays disc golf and reads AMA threads about jobs he&#x27;d never want. 
 Amara Okafor Quora Lead Amara leads Valora&#x27;s Quora presence: finding the questions people actually ask about money and writing answers worth the click. She grew up in Houston in a Nigerian-American household where education was a contact sport, started as a high school teacher, and moved into content strategy after noticing her explainer emails got better responses than the textbook. Her badass credential: she keeps a running map of which money questions trend each month, and it quietly shapes what the whole content team writes next. Outside work she wins pub trivia, bakes bread on a strict schedule, and silently corrects answers at museums. 
 Ava Mercer Facebook Community Lead Ava runs Valora&#x27;s Facebook community: the groups where people trade money questions and answers daily. She&#x27;s from Portland, came up through nonprofit community organizing - the kind where your budget is goodwill and your tools are showing up - and brought that patience to online communities. Her badass credential: she greets new members by name, remembers the regulars, and can defuse a comment-section argument with one well-timed question; community management is mostly gardening, and nobody out-gardens her. Outside work she shoots film photography, volunteers at an actual community garden, and organizes group photos nobody knew they wanted.
